extracted.intended_audience: conference organisers, program/general chairs, and conference peer-review administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing and operating a peer-review model (single-blind, double-blind, open) for academic conferences, comparing pros/cons, operational needs, and empirical effects on reviewer behaviour and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-blind reviewer anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: In a single blind peer review, reviewers’ identities are kept hidden from authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantage: allows reviewers to critique papers without influence, giving them freedom to give an honest critique even when it’s not favourable. Disadvantage: anonymity can enable unusually critical or unprofessional reviews. Empirical note: 85% of respondents had experienced single-blind review, only 52% described it as effective and it was preferred by 25% (Publishing Research Consortium survey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind author anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: In a double blind peer review, the identities of both the authors and reviewers are kept hidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: guards against reviewer influence from an author’s prestige and reduces reviewer bias related to gender, country of origin, academic status, or publication history. Operational requirement: submissions must be prepared to hide authors’ identities fully. Limitations: often imperfect—reviewers may infer authorship from citations, subject area, or writing style. Empirical note: 71% of respondents described double-blind as effective and 56% preferred it in the cited survey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission anonymization practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions must be prepared in a way that hides authors’ identities fully (e.g., avoid repeated self-citations that reveal identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: instruct authors on how to anonymise manuscripts, and ensure your peer-review software supports double-blind workflows. Failure to enforce anonymisation undermines double-blind benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bias dimensions to monitor
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of reviewer bias include influence due to author prestige, gender, country, affiliation, academic status, or previous publication history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chosen review model and operational safeguards to mitigate these biases; the WSDM experiment specifically investigated bias with respect to gender, country, prestige and affiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bidding behaviour and allocation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: How reviewers bid on papers and how bids are weighted/allocated across submissions under different blind conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings from WSDM: single-blind reviewers bid 22% fewer papers on average than double-blind reviewers; single-blind bids were weighted toward submissions from top universities and companies; single-blind reviewers were more likely to submit positive reviews for submissions from prestigious authors or high-quality organisations. Implication: single-blind may increase bids and allocation quality for prominent submissions but can disadvantage lesser-known authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accountability (Open Peer Review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review where identities of authors and reviewers are known and reviews (and responses) are often published alongside the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary goal: maximum transparency and accountability. Pros: increased accountability (discourages unprofessional feedback), educational value (published reviews provide context and learning), and allows reviewers to receive explicit credit. Cons: may cause hesitation among reviewers (fear of retaliation), gentler reviews to preserve relationships, and potential identification even in partially-open models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of retaliation and reviewer hesitation in open review
rubrics_metrics.description: Open review can make early-career or less powerful reviewers reluctant to critique senior or influential researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dynamic can bias reviews toward acceptance and reduce rigorous assessment. Consider protections or mixed models if reviewer candour from junior researchers is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for de-anonymisation across models
rubrics_metrics.description: Even under double-blind conditions (or open-but-anonymous review variants), reviewers can often infer author identities from citations, subject matter, or writing style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that blinding is imperfect in many fields—mitigate by clear anonymisation guidance, conflict-of-interest checks, and realistic expectations about the limits of blinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of software and policy tools to prevent nepotism/conflict of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational measures to prevent nepotism or conflicts of interest, such as blocking matches based on email domain or organisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: ensure review platform can enforce conflict-of-interest rules (e.g., prevent reviewers from being assigned where email domain/organisation indicates a relationship). Combine these measures with double-blind review to strengthen fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer credit and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms to give reviewers explicit credit for their reviewing work (facilitated by open review models).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing credit can be a growing requirement and incentive for high-quality reviews; publishing reviews or attaching reviewer names increases recognition but may trade off with candidness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-offs between reviewer honesty and civility
rubrics_metrics.description: Different review models balance reviewer honesty (willingness to be critical) against civility/constructiveness (professional tone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-blind may promote frank critiques but also permit unusually harsh reviews; open review promotes civility and constructive feedback but can reduce frankness due to social pressures. Choose model according to which trade-off you prioritise and consider moderation policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation for program/general chairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Program and general chairs should consider the advantages of double-blind reviewing when designing conference review processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WSDM experiment authors concluded that conference chairs should 'seriously consider' double-blind reviewing because single-blind conditions allowed reviewers to use author information that can disadvantage some authors; weigh empirical evidence, field norms, and operational feasibility when deciding.
